title: Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Grammar: Form, Structure and Sense
summary: Make every describing phrase point to the right noun: the doer question, appositive openers, the possessive and "of" traps, it/there/passive danglers and misplaced modifiers — with worked examples and a 10-question practice quiz.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Modifier questions are part of **Standard English Conventions**, the grammar-and-punctuation domain of the Reading and Writing section (about 26% of the scored questions, usually 11–15 of them). Inside that domain they belong to the skill called **Form, Structure, and Sense**, which includes **subject–modifier placement** — the official name for what teachers call dangling and misplaced modifiers. Grammar questions usually come after the reading questions in each module, so you will meet them in the second half of Module 1 and again in Module 2.

The question always looks the same: one short text (25–150 words) with a blank, and the stem **"Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?"** In a modifier question, the sentence usually **starts with a describing phrase followed by a comma**, and the blank comes right after that comma. All four choices contain more or less the same words, but each one puts a different noun first. Your job is to pick the choice that starts with the person or thing the opening phrase really describes.

Less often, the blank holds a whole group of words in a different order, and you must choose the order that keeps each describing phrase **next to** the word it describes. That is a misplaced modifier question (Rule 6 below).
First, what is a modifier?

A **modifier** is a word or group of words that describes something else in the sentence. The SAT mostly tests **introductory modifiers**: phrases that open the sentence, end with a comma, and have **no subject of their own**. Because they have no subject, the reader borrows the first noun after the comma as the subject. If that noun cannot logically do or be what the phrase describes, the modifier is **dangling** — it is "hanging" with nothing to hold on to.

rows: After reviewing the data, / By planting trees,
While studying in Paris, / Once dried,
Who was studying? What was dried?
Like her older brother, / Unlike most birds,
Who is like the brother? What is unlike birds?

blocks.text: The answer to the "Ask yourself" question must be the **first noun after the comma** — the subject of the main clause. We call this the **doer question**.
Rule 1: The noun right after the comma must do the action
This one rule answers most modifier questions. Read the opening phrase, decide who or what it describes, and check that this person or thing comes immediately after the comma.

items: ✗ Walking along the Corniche, **the sea breeze** felt cool to Salma. (The breeze was not walking.)
✓ Walking along the Corniche, **Salma** felt the cool sea breeze.
✗ Built in the fourteenth century, **tourists** still visit the mosque every day. (The tourists were not built in the fourteenth century.)
✓ Built in the fourteenth century, **the mosque** still welcomes tourists every day.
✗ Famous for its blue tiles, **visitors** photograph the old school all day. (The visitors are not famous for blue tiles.)
✓ Famous for its blue tiles, **the old school** is photographed by visitors all day.
✗ Once dried, **you** can grind the coffee beans. (You are not dried.)
✓ Once dried, **the coffee beans** can be ground.

blocks.text: Notice the last two ✓ sentences use the passive ("is photographed", "can be ground"). The passive is not wrong in itself. What matters is **which noun comes first**. If the thing being described is the thing that "receives" the action, a passive verb may be exactly what the sentence needs.

Titles and adjectives in front of the noun do not change anything. "Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy", "the young engineer" and "marine biologist Lena Ortiz" all have a person as the head noun, so they are fine after a phrase that describes a person.
Rule 2: An appositive opener renames the noun that follows

An appositive is a noun phrase such as "A former math teacher" or "The oldest university in Africa". When it opens the sentence, it is **another name for the subject**, so the subject must be the **same kind of thing**: a person for a person, a place for a place, an object for an object. Test it by joining them with "is/was": "Hana **was** a former math teacher" makes sense; "Hana's novels **were** a former math teacher" does not.

items: ✗ A former math teacher, **Hana's novels** often include puzzles. (The novels were not a teacher.)
✓ A former math teacher, **Hana** often includes puzzles in her novels.
✗ A city of over twenty million people, **traffic** is a daily challenge in Cairo.
✓ A city of over twenty million people, **Cairo** faces a daily traffic challenge.
✗ The first woman to win the prize, **the committee** praised Dr. Amal Zaki's research.
✓ The first woman to win the prize, **Dr. Amal Zaki** was praised by the committee for her research.

blocks.text: Rule 3: Watch out for possessives and "the ___ of"

The SAT's favourite trap is a choice that **mentions** the right person but does not make that person the subject. In "Hana's novels", the subject is **novels**; Hana only tells us whose novels. In "the research of Dr. Saleh", the subject is **research**. Find the **head noun** — the main noun that the verb belongs to.

items: ✗ Having studied the samples for months, **the scientist's conclusion** was surprising. (head noun = conclusion; a conclusion cannot study)
✓ Having studied the samples for months, **the scientist** reached a surprising conclusion.
✗ Born in Alexandria, **her paintings** often show the sea. ("her" is a possessive too; the head noun is paintings, and paintings were not born.)
✓ Born in Alexandria, **the painter** often shows the sea in her work.
✓ Painted in bright colours, **the temple's columns** attract photographers. (head noun = columns; the columns really were painted, so this possessive is correct)

blocks.text: So a possessive is **not automatically wrong**. Ask: **after the possessive, what is the head noun, and can that noun do or be what the opening phrase says?** Possessive pronouns (his, her, its, their) work exactly like possessive names.
Rule 4: "It", "there" and the passive usually create danglers

Choices that begin with **it is…, there is…**, or a **passive verb with the doer at the end** ("was discovered by the team") push the real doer away from the comma. After an introductory modifier that describes a person, these choices are almost always wrong, even though they may sound formal.

items: ✗ After reviewing the satellite images, **it was clear to the geologists** that a river once flowed there.
✗ After reviewing the satellite images, **there was evidence**, the geologists said, of an old river.
✗ After reviewing the satellite images, **an old river was identified** by the geologists.
✓ After reviewing the satellite images, **the geologists identified** an old river.

blocks.text: The same is true for infinitive openers. "To reduce traffic" needs someone with a goal: "To reduce traffic, **the city** added bus lanes" ✓, not "To reduce traffic, **new bus lanes were added**" ✗ or "To reduce traffic, **it was decided** to add bus lanes" ✗.
Rule 5: When an opener is NOT a dangler
Do not panic at every opening phrase. If the opener is a **full clause with its own subject and verb**, it cannot dangle, so the dangling rule does not decide the answer.

items: ✓ While **Salma was walking** along the Corniche, the sea breeze felt cool. (The opener has its own subject, Salma.)
✓ Because **the beans had dried** in the sun, the farmers could grind them.
✓ **Her experiment finished**, the student cleaned the lab. (an absolute phrase: it has its own noun, "experiment")
✓ In 2019, the museum reopened. / In the desert, water is precious. (short time or place phrases do not need a doer)

blocks.text: In these sentences, use your other grammar tools (verb form, agreement, punctuation) to choose the answer.
Rule 6: Misplaced modifiers in the middle or at the end

A describing phrase should sit **next to** the word it describes. If it is far away, it seems to describe the wrong word, and the sentence becomes illogical or funny. Relative clauses (that…, which…, who…) and prepositional phrases (with…, from…) are the usual troublemakers.

items: ✗ The museum displayed a statue for visitors **carved from a single block of granite**. (The visitors were carved?)
✓ The museum displayed a statue **carved from a single block of granite** for visitors.
✗ Omar found a fossil on his way home **that was 50 million years old**. (His way home was 50 million years old?)
✓ On his way home, Omar found a fossil **that was 50 million years old**.
✗ The nurse gave the medicine to the child **in a small plastic cup** who was crying. (The cup was crying?)
✓ The nurse gave the medicine **in a small plastic cup** to the child **who was crying**.

blocks.text: An -ing phrase at the **end** of a sentence, after a comma, describes the subject of the clause: "The students left the lab, **forgetting** the samples" means the students forgot. If that makes no sense, the phrase is misplaced: "The bus left without us, **running** to the station" ✗ (the bus was running?).

blocks.title: القاعدة اللي لازم تحفظها
items: لو الجملة بادئة بوصف وبعده فاصلة (Walking… / Built… / A former teacher…)، اسأل نفسك: مين اللي بيعمل الحاجة دي؟
الإجابة لازم تكون أول اسم بعد الفاصلة على طول. لو أول اسم مش هو اللي بيعمل الفعل، الاختيار غلط.
خلي بالك من الملكية: Hana's novels الفاعل فيها novels مش Hana. وأي اختيار بيبدأ بـ it أو there غالبًا غلط.

blocks.text: The 3-step method for test day

items: **Read the opening phrase and ask the doer question.** "Having analysed the recordings" → who analysed? Answer in your head before you read the choices: the biologist.

**Look only at the first noun of each choice.** Cross out every choice whose head noun is not your answer. Check for possessives ("the biologist's study"), "the ___ of", "it", "there" and passives that move the doer to the end.
**Check the survivor in the full sentence.** The verb must agree with the subject and the sentence must be complete. Usually only one choice survives step 2.

blocks.text: You often do **not** need to read the whole passage. The sentence before the blank helps you understand the topic, but the grammar decision is made inside the sentence with the blank.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1: a participle phrase**

Humpback whales are famous for their long, complex songs, which can last for hours. Having analyzed more than two thousand recordings of these songs from the Indian Ocean, ______ that the songs change gradually from one season to the next.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) the conclusion of marine biologist Lena Ortiz was
B) marine biologist Lena Ortiz concluded
C) it was concluded by marine biologist Lena Ortiz
D) marine biologist Lena Ortiz's conclusion was

blocks.title: Answer: B) marine biologist Lena Ortiz concluded
items: Doer question: who analyzed the recordings? A person — Lena Ortiz. Choice B puts "marine biologist Lena Ortiz" right after the comma, and "concluded that…" completes the sentence.
A is wrong: the head noun is "conclusion". A conclusion cannot analyze recordings ("the ___ of" trap).
C is wrong: "it" comes after the comma, and the passive "was concluded by" hides the doer at the end (it/passive trap).
D is wrong: in "Lena Ortiz's conclusion" the possessive makes "conclusion" the subject, not Lena Ortiz (possessive trap).

blocks.text: **Worked example 2: an appositive opener**

Many farms in southern Egypt depend on diesel pumps that are costly to run. A self-taught engineer from Aswan, ______ a low-cost solar water pump that small farms can repair using parts sold in local markets.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) the design by Karim Nassar is
B) it was Karim Nassar who designed
C) Karim Nassar designed
D) Karim Nassar's design is

blocks.title: Answer: C) Karim Nassar designed
items: The appositive "A self-taught engineer from Aswan" renames a person, so a person must come after the comma. Choice C gives "Karim Nassar designed a low-cost solar water pump" — complete and logical.
A is wrong: the subject is "the design", and a design is not an engineer ("the ___ of/by" trap).
B is wrong: the subject is "it". The sentence now says "it" was a self-taught engineer (it/there trap).
D is wrong: "Karim Nassar's design" has the head noun "design" again (possessive trap).

blocks.text: **Worked example 3: when the possessive is correct**

Restorers in Cairo spent two years cleaning an ancient statue that had been stored in a basement since the 1930s. Carved from a single block of red granite, ______ now stands in the museum's main courtyard.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) the work of the restorers
B) the pharaoh's statue
C) the restorers' cleaning of the statue
D) it is the statue that

blocks.title: Answer: B) the pharaoh's statue
items: Doer question: what was carved from granite? The statue. In B the head noun is "statue" ("the pharaoh's" only tells us whose statue), so the possessive is fine here: "the pharaoh's statue now stands in the courtyard."
A is wrong: the head noun is "work". The restorers' work was not carved from granite ("the ___ of" trap).
C is wrong: the head noun is "cleaning", which cannot be carved.
D is wrong: it starts with "it", so the sentence says "it" was carved (it/there trap). It is also wordy.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4: a misplaced modifier**
A small bakery in Tanta has become famous online for its early-morning queues. Every day, the owner ______.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) sells bread to customers fresh from the oven who wait in line before sunrise
B) sells bread fresh from the oven to customers who wait in line before sunrise
C) sells bread to customers who wait in line before sunrise fresh from the oven
D) fresh from the oven, sells bread to customers who wait in line before sunrise

blocks.title: Answer: B) sells bread fresh from the oven to customers who wait in line before sunrise
items: "Fresh from the oven" describes the bread, so it must sit right after "bread"; "who wait in line" describes the customers, so it must sit right after "customers". Only B keeps both modifiers next to their words.
A is wrong: "customers fresh from the oven" — the customers were baked?
C is wrong: "fresh from the oven" now follows "sunrise" and seems to describe the customers or the sunrise.
D is wrong: the phrase now describes "the owner", who is not fresh from the oven.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **The possessive trap:** "the scientist's discovery", "her paintings" — the possessive word is not the subject; the noun after it is.
**The "of" trap:** "the work of the scientist" — the subject is "work".
**The it/there trap:** "it was found that…", "there were…" right after an opening modifier.
**The hidden-doer passive:** "the results were published by the team" — the team is at the end, so "the results" become the doer.
**The wrong-person trap:** a choice that starts with a person, but the wrong person (readers, visitors, the committee) instead of the one described.
**The sounds-formal trap:** a long, academic-sounding choice is not better. Short and active is usually right.
**The far-away modifier:** a that/which/who clause or a with/from phrase separated from its noun.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: See an opening phrase + comma + blank? It is a modifier question. Ask "Who or what did this?" before you look at the choices.
Scan only the head noun of each choice; three choices usually fall at once.
Distrust choices starting with it, there, the ___ of, or a possessive name — but check the head noun before you reject a possessive.
If the opener has its own subject (While she was…, Because the beans…), the dangling rule does not apply; look for another error.
For word-order choices, put each describing phrase right next to its noun.
These questions are quick. Answer in 30–45 seconds and save time for the reading questions.

blocks.title: الوصف لازم يكون جنب صاحبه
blocks.text: في الـ misplaced modifier الوصف بيبقى في نص الجملة أو في آخرها بس بعيد عن الكلمة اللي بيوصفها. حط كل وصف جنب الاسم بتاعه على طول: bread fresh from the oven و customers who wait in line. لو الوصف بقى جنب اسم تاني والمعنى بقى غريب أو يضحك، يبقى الاختيار غلط.
Practice

blocks.title: Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers — Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 10 questions in Digital SAT format. Untimed: ask the doer question before you look at the choices, then check your answer and read every explanation.

questions.p: Spacecraft returning from orbit enter Earth's atmosphere at very high speed, and friction heats their outer surfaces. Designed to withstand temperatures above 1,000°C, ______ protect the spacecraft during this dangerous part of the journey.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: engineers created ceramic tiles to
the purpose of the ceramic tiles is to
ceramic tiles
the job of ceramic tiles is to
questions.e: The tiles were designed to withstand heat, so "ceramic tiles" must follow the comma (C). A makes engineers the thing designed to withstand heat; B and D make "purpose" and "job" the subject.

questions.p: The Nile has shaped life in northeastern Africa for thousands of years. Stretching about 6,700 kilometers from its sources to the Mediterranean Sea, ______ to farms and cities in many countries.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: water is supplied by the Nile River
the Nile River supplies water
the Nile River's water is supplied
the water of the Nile River goes
questions.e: The river is what stretches 6,700 km, so "the Nile River" must come right after the comma (B). In A, C and D the head noun is "water", which does not stretch from the sources to the sea.

questions.p: Buildings in the city can apply for a green rating that recognizes energy-saving design. To earn the gold rating from the city's green-building council, ______ at least 40 percent of its electricity from renewable sources.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the council requires that a building produce
producing is required of a building for
it is necessary for a building to produce
a building must produce
questions.e: The building is the one trying to earn the rating, so "a building" must be the subject (D). A makes the council earn its own rating; B begins with "producing" and C with "it", neither of which can earn a rating.

questions.p: Visitors to the ancient temple are often surprised to learn that its stone was once brightly colored. Originally painted in vivid reds and blues, ______ have faded to soft pastel shades over the centuries.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the temple's carved columns
the colors on the temple's columns
visitors now see that the temple's columns
time has caused the temple's columns to
questions.e: The head noun in A is "columns", and the columns really were painted, so this possessive is correct. B makes "colors" painted in colors, C makes visitors painted and D makes time painted.

questions.p: Scientists have long suspected that rivers once flowed across what is now Egypt's Western Desert. After reviewing high-resolution satellite images of the region, ______ ancient riverbeds buried several meters beneath the sand.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: evidence was found by geologists of
the geologists' findings revealed
geologists found evidence of
there was evidence, geologists said, of
questions.e: The geologists reviewed the images, so they must follow the comma (C). A is passive with "evidence" first, B makes "findings" review images (possessive trap), and D starts with "there".

questions.p: Huda Mansour did not publish her first book until late in life. A former schoolteacher who began writing at the age of fifty, ______ into eleven languages, and her stories are now studied in several universities.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Huda Mansour's novels about village life have been translated
Huda Mansour has had her novels about village life translated
the novels of Huda Mansour about village life have been translated
village life is the subject of Huda Mansour's novels, translated
questions.e: The appositive describes a person, so Huda Mansour must be the subject, as in B. A (possessive) and C ("the novels of") make the novels a schoolteacher; D makes village life a schoolteacher.

questions.p: Some young writers in Cairo are experimenting with the way characters speak on the page. Written in a mix of Arabic and English, ______ reflects the bilingual way many young Egyptians actually talk with their friends.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the novel's dialogue
readers find that the novel's dialogue
the author chose dialogue that
it is the novel's dialogue that
questions.e: The dialogue was written in a mix of Arabic and English, so "the novel's dialogue" (head noun: dialogue) must follow the comma (A). B makes readers written, C makes the author written, and D starts with "it".

questions.p: During a long drought, an ancient olive tree in Siwa lost almost all its leaves, and many people believed it had died. Having survived two dry summers without rain, ______ surprised scientists by producing new green shoots within a week of the first rain.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the ancient olive tree's recovery
the shoots of the ancient olive tree
the recovery of the ancient olive tree
the ancient olive tree
questions.e: The tree survived the dry summers, so "the ancient olive tree" must be the subject (D). A and C make the recovery survive two summers; B makes the new shoots, which had not grown yet, survive them.

questions.p: In a recent interview, the director of a small museum in Fayoum described the collection's newest object. According to the director, the museum acquired ______.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: a bronze mirror from a private collector that is nearly 2,500 years old
from a private collector that is nearly 2,500 years old a bronze mirror
a bronze mirror that is nearly 2,500 years old from a private collector
nearly 2,500 years old, a bronze mirror from a private collector
questions.e: "That is nearly 2,500 years old" describes the mirror, so it must follow "a bronze mirror" directly (C). In A the clause follows "collector", so the collector seems 2,500 years old; B puts the clause after "collector" and scrambles the order; D leaves the age phrase with no noun to describe.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Misplaced modifiers

questions.p: Many students in Cairo spend more than an hour commuting to school each day. To cut that time in half, ______ a network of express school buses that would stop only at major squares.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the transport ministry has proposed
there is now a proposal by the transport ministry for
it has been proposed by the transport ministry that the city build
the transport ministry's proposal includes
questions.e: An infinitive of purpose ("To cut that time") needs someone with a goal right after the comma: the transport ministry (A). B starts with "there", C with "it", and D has the head noun "proposal" (possessive trap).

blocks.title: Remember
items: An opening phrase + comma must be followed by the noun that does or is the action — ask the doer question first.
Find the head noun: in "the scientist's conclusion" or "the work of the scientist" the subject is not the scientist.
Choices starting with it or there, or a passive that hides the doer at the end, are the usual wrong answers.
An opener with its own subject (While she was…) cannot dangle — look for another error.
Keep every describing phrase right next to the word it describes.
